title: Rerank service: concurrency sharding, token ceilings, and timeout tuning
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Improve latency and throughput of the /rerank endpoint by introducing request-level concurrency sharding, enforcing token ceilings per candidate, and tightening timeout/early-exit heuristics. Current behaviour serializes scoring over candidates and suffers on long candidate lists and token-heavy inputs; goal is to reduce 95th percentile latency by 40% for common workloads and maintain top-k quality within a 0.5% delta.
acceptance_criteria: 95th percentile latency for standard rerank request (50 candidates, avg 12 tokens) reduced by >= 35% compared to baseline (runtime-1.20).
End-to-end top-5 ranking quality (NDCG@5) difference <= 0.5% vs baseline on our surf-test prompt set.
No regressions in token-level cost > +5% per request on average across bench workloads.
New configuration flags available: rerank.parallel_shards (int), rerank.per_candidate_token_limit (int), rerank.early_exit_ms (int).
E2E integration tests and canary rollout plan documented in Confluence and configured in the console rollout UI.
tasks: Design concurrency sharding algorithm: static shard assignment vs dynamic worker pool
Implement per-candidate token trimming before tokenization to reduce tokenization overhead
Add early-exit aggregator: stop scoring remaining candidates when top-k stable for X ms
Expose runtime flags and config via API+console (shards, token_limit, timeout_ms)
Update SDKs and add guidance to prompts about token limits for rerank endpoints
Benchmark: run pipeline across small/medium/large candidate lists and measure p50/p95/p99
Create canary rollout (10% traffic) with rollback hooks and observability dashboards
notes: Trade-offs considered: static sharding simplifies ordering determinism but may underutilize GPUs for skewed candidate distributions; dynamic worker pool improves throughput but complicates top-k merging and consistency guarantees.

We decided to implement an initial hybrid approach: request-level shard count derived from candidate_count and average token estimate; each shard scored in parallel with bounded worker slots per-device.

Per-candidate token trimming will be a best-effort heuristic: if token_count > per_candidate_token_limit, trim to prefix+suffix (configurable) and mark candidate as truncated for downstream explanations.

Early-exit aggregator uses a stability window (default 40ms) where top-k doesn't change after scoring an additional N candidates; this avoids waiting for long tails while preserving quality on typical distributions.
We will ship conservative defaults (shards=4, token_limit=128, early_exit_ms=40) and iterate based on canary telemetry.
Benchmarks to run include: synthetic worst-case (500 candidates, avg 256 tokens), real-customer mixes (support tickets corpus), and small fast lists (10 candidates).

outstanding_risks: Long-tail inputs with many high-token candidates may still produce high latency despite parallelism; mitigation: advertise input limits and provide SDK helpers to pre-trim candidates.
Complexity in merging partial top-k from shards could introduce subtle nondeterminism; mitigation: deterministic merge based on seed and stable sort on scores+candidate_id.
Increased concurrency could surface new memory pressure on PKVS (per-request caches); mitigation: bounded cache size and eviction LRU per-request.
